Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Iași has become the first county in Romania where all local authorities have decided to ban gambling halls with slot machines, following a civic campaign that gathered more than 7,000 signatures. The local councils of all 98 cities and communes in Iași County voted to prohibit gambling halls under powers granted to local authorities by recent legislation, making the county the first in the country to adopt such a comprehensive ban. Implementation will vary across municipalities. Some local councils have opted to close gambling halls immediately, while others will allow existing licences to expire. According to the National Office for Gambling, the last licences in the county are due to expire in February 2027. The initiative was driven by a county-wide civic campaign that argued gambling addiction had become a significant social problem. "The ordinance moved the decision to local authorities. We were very happy because it is easier to convince a city hall than a government to legislate," civic activist Paul Ciobanu said, as quoted by Digi24 . "We can be happy that we are the first county to get rid of this phenomenon. We started with 'Iași – Say no to the scoundrels', and then another 170 local campaigns appeared." Supporters of the ban said it would help reduce gambling addiction and its social consequences. Some residents who previously struggled with gambling welcomed the decision, saying their financial losses had far exceeded any winnings. The Iași initiative could serve as a model for other Romanian counties, as the legislative framework now allows local councils to decide whether to authorise gambling halls within their jurisdictions. In related news, residents of a neighbourhood in Timisoara have protested City Hall’s proposal to relocate all the gambling halls from the city to their area. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life.text: Every place, country, city or town has its unique landmark that visitors seek out. For example, Rome in Italy has Trevi Fountain where people toss coins and make a wish. In Prague, they touch historic statues for luck. But in Hungary's capital, Budapest, travellers line up for hours just to rub the belly of a happy-looking bronze statue of a policeman. And they do so because it is believed to bring good luck, prosperity, happiness and safe journeys.Who is this Fat Policeman In Budapest, it is simply known as the Fat Policeman Statue. Itâs a quirky bronze figure which has become one of Budapest's most photographed attractions. Even from far, you can see his shiny rounded belly which shimmers like polished gold. It shines because thousands of hands touch it every year in the hope of receiving a little luck.A travel superstition or not, this smiling policeman statue has become a delightful ritual for visitors exploring Budapest. There are several videos on Instagram, which shows travellers rubbing the fat belly of the statue.Where is the Fat Policeman Statue? The statue stands in the heart of Budapest, at the corner of ZrÃ­nyi Street (ZrÃ­nyi utca) and OktÃ³ber 6 Street (OktÃ³ber 6. utca). For more precise location, itâs just a short walk from St. Stephen's Basilica. The statue can be located easily as visitors can also reach here from the iconic Chain Bridge.The reason behind the belly rub The biggest attraction isn't the statue itself but the tradition surrounding it. As per local belief, rubbing the policeman's belly brings good luck and financial prosperity. It also means safe travels. Some locals also jokingly say it ensures you'll return to Budapest one day, and another legend claims it prevents you from gaining weight. But these are folk beliefs rather than historical facts which have become a prominent part of Budapest travel.Who does the statue represent? Affectionately known as the "Fat Policeman," the bronze sculpture is a life-sized figure depicting a jovial Hungarian policeman. He is wearing a ceremonial uniform inspired by the early 20th century. He also wears a helmet to complete the look. Rather than celebrating law enforcement, the statue captures a humorous side of the city.The present sculpture credits Hungarian sculptor AndrÃ¡s IllyÃ©s and notes the present bronze work was unveiled in 2008.How to reach the statue Nearest landmark: St. Stephen's Basilica (just a one-minute walk)Nearest metro station: Bajcsy-Zsilinszky Ãºt (M1 Metro), around five minutes walkFrom Chain Bridge: Around a 7â10 minute walkFrom the Hungarian Parliament Building: Around 15 minutes on footBecause it sits in Budapest's pedestrian-friendly city centre, most travellers simply discover it while exploring nearby attractions.Best time to visit for photographyFor best photographs and no waiting in line, come as early as possible in the morning or later in the evening. Why travellers love it Visitors love it because they can interact with it. Every person who places a hand on its polished belly becomes part of a tradition and shared experience from around the world. So, if Budapest is on your travel bucket list, don't rush past this smiling bronze officer. Smile for a pic, rub the famous shiny belly for money and luck.Looking for trusted parenting advice? Photograph: Museum of Villena/EPA Art theft Bronze age treasure stolen in four-minute Spanish museum heist Gold collection known as Treasure of Villena, worth at least €1.7m, is target of ‘very well planned’ raid Philip Oltermann and agencies Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.47 EDT First published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 07.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thieves in Spain have raided the Treasure of Villena – a stunning collection of bronze age gold artefacts that has been described as the most important prehistoric trove in Europe – in the latest high-profile smash-and-grab heist on the continent. The raid on Thursday morning of the 66 mostly gold objects in the Spanish town of Villena lasted just minutes, officials said. “The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5.20am [4.20am BST],” a spokesperson for the town council said, adding that the thieves had left the building by 5.24am. The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, the spokesperson said. “They’ve taken most of the treasure,” the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdán, told journalists, his voice breaking. View image in fullscreen The collection has been held in a specially designated room in the Museum of Villena since May 2024. Photograph: Pablo Miranzo/EPA Local media said the few items the thieves had left behind included three silver vessels, a bracelet and some of the ornamentation of the bastón del reyezuelo, the “Kingfisher staff”, a prehistoric ceremonial scepter. Cerdán said: “We are absolutely devastated, I’m even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It’s part of our heritage, of our wealth.” The treasure, which was discovered in 1963 by the archaeologist José María Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena, included 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles and other miscellaneous pieces dating back to about 1000BC. It immediately became the main attraction of a small architectural museum in the province of Alicante. Since May 2024, the hoard has been on display in a specially designated room in the newly opened, municipally owned Villena Museum. The unusual material of some of the items has long intrigued researchers. Though mainly gold, some pieces are also made of silver, iron, amber and a dark leaden material covered in a ferrous-looking oxide. A recent study published in the journal Trabajos de Prehistoria claimed that these items were probably forged from rare meteoritic iron. While the treasure’s value is incalculable, the gold alone is worth about €1.7m (£1.45m), according to the mayor. The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum through a window, according to the Spanish government’s deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda. “All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesperson, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum. Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were now investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added. Mauro Hernández, a professor of archaeology at the University of Alicante and an expert on the treasure, told the broadcaster Cadena SER that the operation showed signs of prior planning. “They had it very well planned,” Hernández said. “They knew how to do it, how to act and how to escape.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Guns, axes, explosives: violent museum heists are on the rise, says Europol Read more Last October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewellery worth €88m. There have since been a series of brazen raids in institutions across Europe. Four works “of extraordinary value” by the Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily, Italy’s culture ministry said last Sunday. Two days earlier, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m which were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation Museum near Parma. In a report published at the start of the week, the EU’s police agency Europol said that member states had detected a recent shift “towards violent and forceful methods” that could point to the involvement of new criminal networks focused on specific cultural artefacts. “Some thieves apprehended in recent cases appear to coordinate their efforts on an ad hoc basis, often recruited locally through social media and instant communication channels, without prior connections to each other,” the report said. “This differs from the usual structure of criminal networks involved in cultural goods trafficking, which typically operate in a core group organised around a leader.” Agence France-Presse contributed to this report Explore more on these topics Art theft Museums Spain Organised crime Europe Heritage news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Alleged crime boss Daniel Kinahan’s return to Ireland ends global game of cat-and-mouse Italian police recover paintings by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse after heist Portrait looted by Nazis found in home of Dutch SS leader’s family Fears Quebec Starbucks gang shooting could signal shift to brazen tactics ‘A wow moment’: ancient Romanian gold helmet returned in plea deal with theft suspects Italian fugitive caught after passion for football betrays his location Thieves steal Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse paintings worth millions from Italian museum Richard Wakeling, crime boss extradited to UK from Thailand, starts jail sentence Louvre heist: hunt on for thieves after eight ‘priceless’ jewellery pieces stolen British organised crime boss arrested in Thailand Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
